title: Ep 288: LawDroid Founder Tom Martin on Building, Teaching and Advising About AI for Legal
author: Tom Martin

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Martin does not substantively engage the cluster’s central concern that automation may erode apprenticeship and leave juniors unable to verify AI output. Instead, he reframes AI’s labour impact around differentiated legal roles, transitional disruption, proactive practice and demand expansion, offering predictions rather than a training or competence-reproduction response.
qs: I mean, clearly, I want to be transparent with everyone that in the short term, there's going to be a lot of change where when it gets changed from this one view of what a lawyer is to a lawyer being many different things or different types of legal positions available, that there's going to be a period of transition where we're all getting up to speed.

And then, yes, you may lose a little bit on the billable hours for reactive work, but if you could go extremely deeply into a company's day to day operations on a proactive side, you could not only offset, but probably expand the book of business that you have.

st.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes
st.an: The source does not address the cluster’s proposition about cautious AI adoption, customer outcomes, provider collaboration or distributed expertise. Its brief endorsement of rebelliousness and personal anecdote provide insufficient evidence to determine alignment.

st.an: Martin offers implementation guidance on buy-versus-build decisions and using vendors’ accumulated experience, which aligns with the cluster’s concern that adoption requires expertise. st.an: Martin treats corporate legal teams as AI adopters and recommends leveraging vendors’ accumulated implementation experience, which is relevant to the cluster’s deployment themes. st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: The source contains no substantive legal-AI claims, evidence, predictions or recommendations, so it does not establish a position on pragmatic adoption, experimentation or whether transformation remains forecast rather than demonstrated.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source accepts that AI can broaden legal help beyond one-to-one representation and materially develops the proposition by proposing lawyer-built, reliability-grounded alternatives to public general-purpose tools. It also adds a commercial incentive for lawyers, though its access and business benefits remain predictions rather than measured justice-gap outcomes.

st.t: Production model: Institutional absorption governs AI value
st.an: Martin accepts that AI’s value requires lawyer-led redesign rather than mere tool access, and materially extends the cluster by proposing one-to-many delivery and proactive, real-time advice as new service and revenue models. His claims reinforce the cluster’s scenarios for access, pricing and changing roles, but remain largely predictive rather than evidence of measured outcomes.

st.an: Martin supports redesigning legal service around proactive, continuous client involvement rather than reactive billable work. st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Martin supports the cluster’s framing of AI as reshaping legal roles and service delivery rather than simply replacing lawyers. st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: Martin accepts the cluster’s core proposition that generative AI can help narrow the justice gap, and the host cites his work with legal-aid organisations and courts. However, the excerpt offers no mechanisms, outcomes, or engagement with the cluster’s central concerns about verification, remedies, inequality, and safeguards.
qs: Tom has worked extensively with Legal Aid Organizations and Courts to leverage AI technology in making Legal Services more accessible.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Martin supports the cluster’s core view that generative AI broadens legal software capabilities while specialist value comes from lawyer-oriented workflow design, accessible interfaces and implementation support. He frames LawDroid primarily as a copilot that simplifies defined tasks for lawyers, acknowledges imperfect outputs and offers consulting to aid adoption; however, his support rests on development experience and product claims rather than comparative performance evidence.
qs: One is called Copilot, which everyone is familiar with now, that helps lawyers to do their jobs.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: Martin supports the cluster’s lawyer-guided augmentation framing through a practitioner example in which AI agents automate repetitive communications while existing staff move to higher-value work. His legal-aid account also supports expanded capacity, but his evidence is anecdotal and unquantified and does not establish autonomous delivery or broad transformation.

But what they're able to actually use that same staff for internally is for stuff that's much more high level, that's much more valuable, both for their insurance company as well as the attorneys they work with.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Martin supports the proposition that AI will reorganise legal production and roles rather than eliminate lawyers wholesale. He predicts differentiated legal careers, reduced reactive billable work offset by more proactive services, and staff redeployment to higher-value tasks, while grounding some claims only in client anecdotes and forecasts rather than measured market-wide evidence.

st.t: Service redesign: Resistance reflects incentives and identity
st.an: Martin broadly supports the cluster’s view that legal-AI uptake depends on changes in professional habits and receptiveness, not capability alone. His pandemic account identifies disruption of entrenched routines as an adoption catalyst, but he does not develop the cluster’s fuller analysis of incentives, leadership, workflows, data or multidisciplinary implementation.

st.an: Martin supports the proposition that AI can substitute for some legal work while complementing lawyers and reshaping roles and business models. kp.k: Generative AI replaces conditional chatbots with fluid conversation
kp.d: Martin contrasts his earlier natural-language chatbot, which used conditional logic to answer questions, with generative AI's more human, fluid conversation. He describes incorporating generative AI after ChatGPT's November 2022 launch as an additional layer of capability, while acknowledging limitations and his own learning curve.
qs: But it was pretty much conditional logic behind the scenes.
So this really opened the door to have a much more human, fluid conversation
I certainly experienced that it wasn't perfect.

kp.k: Simplified interfaces and no-code tools broaden legal AI use
kp.d: Martin describes LawDroid Copilot as a curated interface for lawyers who lack time or interest in prompt engineering, offering summarization and counterargument generation. He describes Builder as a no-code platform for custom AI agents, including phone answering, website lead capture, client interviewing and document creation. These are the vendor founder's product descriptions, including his assertions of privacy and security.
qs: My bet on that was most lawyers, they don't want to get up to speed or have the time to spend learning prompt engineering.
It's a more simplified version of ChatGPT that's secure and private for lawyers' use.

We even have templates where you can build up like a phone assistant to answer your phones for you, one for your website to capture leads, one that can interview clients and actually create documents for you.

kp.k: Implementation should start with concrete organizational value
kp.d: Martin recommends identifying a concrete organizational problem and its value before selecting or expanding an AI project. He regards experimentation as useful for opening minds but criticizes abstract vendor use cases that are not connected to firm benefits. This is implementation advice rather than a measured finding.
qs: One of my pet peeves is when vendors talk about use cases.
It's not really tied to what value it's creating for your firm.
you really have to think of a concrete problem that you're solving that creates value for the organization.

kp.k: Vendor experience can inform build-versus-buy decisions
kp.d: Martin argues that firms building custom systems can overlook issues already encountered by legal AI vendors across clients. He also asserts that lessons from his access-to-justice work apply to corporate legal roles and big law. These recommendations arise from his consulting and vendor experience, not a comparative evaluation of internal and purchased systems.
qs: You see sometimes when law firms spin up their own custom build that they miss a lot of things.
When you work with a legal AI vendor, we've been through all of these lessons many, many times over with many different clients.
a lot of the lessons learned that I have over the years in more of the A to J space, they apply with equal measure to the space in corporate and big law.

kp.k: Treat AI as a fallible assistant, not an oracle
kp.d: Martin emphasizes mindset before strategy: lawyers should regard AI as assistance requiring human checking rather than a magical authority. He attributes the incident he calls the Schwartz case to an oracle mindset and claims that treating AI as a fallible assistant would have prevented it. That causal explanation is his interpretation, not a finding established in the interview.
qs: And mindset comes even before strategy.
a lot of people have made the mistake of looking at AI as an oracle, something magical.
That's why the Schwartz case happened, because that was the mindset.
If the mindset was, it's a helpful assistant, assistants make mistakes, we need to look at this, then that wouldn't have happened.

kp.k: AI may diversify legal roles amid transitional disruption
kp.d: Martin credits Richard Susskind with anticipating differentiated legal roles and endorses a move away from a single artisanal conception of the lawyer. He predicts changing skill definitions and opportunities to specialize by strength, but warns of short-term growing pains. He calls job-elimination rhetoric partly vendor-driven hype without ruling out substantial changes to existing jobs; no employment estimates or specific occupational disappearance dates are supplied.

in the short term, there's going to be a lot of change

as lawyers are currently defined, yeah, that's probably going to go away, but there's going to be many more opportunities.

kp.d: Martin predicts that AI could enable ongoing legal analysis using real-time organizational information, shifting lawyers from reactive firefighting toward deeper daily involvement in clients' businesses. He suggests that expanded proactive work could offset or exceed lost billable hours from reactive work. This is a proposed business-development mechanism, not reported revenue evidence or a specific alternative pricing model.

kp.d: Martin argues that multilingual communication, immediate translation and adaptation to users' comprehension levels can improve access to justice. kp.k: Issue identification could expand access and legal demand
kp.d: Martin proposes that conversational AI could identify legal issues users do not recognize, suggest next steps and direct them to resources. He presents this as moving beyond one-to-one representation toward one-to-many assistance and potentially generating business for lawyers. His reference to 92% of the population is unsupported by a named study or denominator explanation in this transcript and remains part of his argument, not an established population finding.

We've been stuck with the one-to-one legal representation model. This opens up one to many
if you can identify all these issues and potential legal cases that you didn't even know existed before for 92% of the population, that's going to lead to more business.

kp.k: Lawyers should offer reliable alternatives to public chatbots
kp.d: Host Bob Ambrogi raises the danger that natural, empathetic chat interfaces may cause users to forget they are interacting with AI. Martin responds that public systems already answer legal questions and recommends lawyers provide better alternatives using information they know is accurate. He connects that recommendation to the profession's social responsibilities rather than advocating resistance to public AI use.
qs: probably one of the greatest dangers is people using an AI-generated chat interface and losing track of the fact they're talking to AI.
ChatGPT is out there. You know, Claude is out there every single day answering questions like this.

we're here not only to make money and have a business, but also to benefit society and help people.

kp.d: Martin reports that an unnamed international legal insurer uses chatbots and AI agents to handle recurring communications with a US network of over 15,000 lawyers, work previously performed manually. He claims time savings and avoided additional staffing, with existing staff redirected to higher-value work. This is an unquantified vendor customer anecdote; the transcript does not isolate the contribution of generative AI from other chatbot automation.

kp.k: Legal AI education combines theory with implementation planning
kp.d: Martin describes his Suffolk course, Generative AI and the Delivery of Legal Services, as a 13-week program covering history, ethics, practical examples and access to justice, supported by workbook exercises, NotebookLM podcasts, mini lectures and a chatbot tutor trained on the chapters. Its capstone requires an AI implementation plan for a law firm, intended to give students a practical artifact they can bring into employment rather than only experience experimenting with tools.
qs: I had to construct an entire 13 week course.
the background about Generative AI, the history, ethics, real world use cases and examples, access to justice.
I created, of course, a Chatbot tutor that was trained on all of the different chapters and then could actually tutor the students through the concepts.
the Capstone project that I assigned to them at the beginning of the semester is for them to put together an AI implementation plan for a law firm.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Martin says generative AI makes legal chatbots more conversational and allows lawyers to use AI assistance without learning prompt engineering.
pts.d: Contrasting generative AI with his earlier conditional-logic chatbot, Tom Martin describes more fluid interaction. He says LawDroid Copilot packages prompting into buttons for tasks such as summarization and counterargument generation, and describes it as secure and private. He also says LawDroid Builder supports no-code creation of custom AI agents, including phone answering, website lead capture, client interviewing and document creation. These are the founder's descriptions of current product capabilities, not independently tested performance findings. LawDroid is a software vendor in these examples.

pts.k: Martin argues that successful AI implementation depends on solving concrete organizational problems rather than adopting abstract use cases or expecting a magical solution.
pts.d: He presents problem definition and value creation as prerequisites for moving beyond experimentation into organizational deployment. He also claims that experienced legal-AI vendors can save firms time and effort relative to custom builds that repeat previously solved problems. This is implementation advice grounded in his vendor and consulting experience; he does not offer comparative cost or deployment-success data.

pts.k: Martin advocates treating AI as a fallible assistant requiring human checking, rather than as an authoritative oracle.
pts.d: He attributes the incident he calls the 'Schwartz case' to an oracle mindset and argues that treating AI as an assistant whose work must be checked would have prevented it. This is his causal interpretation of a court incident, not a measured error rate or demonstrated causal finding. His preferred framing is lawyer augmentation with verification, rather than uncritical reliance on AI output.

pts.k: Martin predicts differentiated legal roles, changing job definitions and short-term disruption, followed by broader opportunities.
pts.d: Martin explicitly adopts the role-differentiation outlook he credits to Richard Susskind: the unitary lawyer role will give way to more varied legal positions that accommodate different strengths. He does not identify particular occupations that will disappear or give displacement numbers. Although he calls job-elimination rhetoric partly hype, he also predicts that lawyers' current job definitions will probably disappear. His own forecast includes transition costs, not a categorical promise that all existing jobs will survive.

pts.k: Martin predicts that AI-enabled proactive advice could offset lost reactive billable work and expand lawyers' business.
pts.d: He envisages real-time legal analysis of feedback from corporate operations, allowing lawyers to become more deeply involved in clients' day-to-day business. He predicts that this could compensate for reduced billable hours on reactive matters and potentially increase the book of business. This is a conditional commercial forecast, not a report of measured revenue gains or a claim that hourly billing will necessarily disappear.

pts.k: Martin says conversational, multilingual AI can make legal self-help more accessible and scale legal-aid services.
pts.d: He identifies translation, adaptation to users' comprehension levels and training on reliable legal-aid or court information as mechanisms for improving guidance. He reports work with the Tennessee Alliance for Legal Services and Tennessee Supreme Court that guides users through questions to generate forms and can take electronic signatures. He argues that these capabilities make services accessible through conversation and move delivery beyond a one-to-one representation model. The Tennessee example is reported deployment experience; the wider justice-gap impact is a claimed opportunity without quantified outcome evidence.

pts.k: Martin predicts that AI conversations can uncover unrecognized legal problems and generate additional demand for lawyers.
pts.d: He suggests that AI can classify issues emerging in approachable conversations, alert users that they may have legal problems and direct them to resources. He then predicts that identifying previously unseen cases will create more business for lawyers. His reference to '92% of the population' is not sourced or defined in the interview and should not be treated as an established population-level measure. Identifying unmet civil legal need and converting it into paying work are related but distinct claims; no conversion evidence is provided.

pts.k: Martin reports that an insurer's AI-assisted lawyer support saved staff time and enabled staff redeployment to higher-value work.
pts.d: He describes an unnamed international legal insurer with a US network of over 15,000 lawyers. Previously manual handling of recurring questions was supported by chatbots and AI agents that interpreted requests, answered questions, directed users and sometimes resolved problems. Martin reports avoided additional staffing and redeployment of existing staff, rather than layoffs. Although offered in response to a question about generative AI, he describes the implementation broadly as chatbots and AI agents and does not isolate the contribution of generative AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The interview primarily offers Martin's product-development and consulting experience, illustrative deployments and forward-looking reasoning.
pts.d: The strongest concrete examples are the named Tennessee form-completion work and the unnamed insurer's support workflow. Neither includes before-and-after measurements, independent evaluation, accuracy benchmarks, costs or user-outcome data. The insurer's network size describes deployment context, not measured productivity. Product capabilities are founder testimony. Martin invokes Susskind as an intellectual influence on role differentiation and the Schwartz incident as support for verification. His National Law Review articles are mentioned but their supporting evidence is not reproduced. Forecasts about richer careers, expanded business and broad justice-gap effects remain predictions in this source. Host remarks and sponsor advertisements are not treated as evidence for Martin's claims.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Martin distinguishes existing capabilities and deployments from undated future transformation, with short-term growing pains and implementation conditions.
pts.d: In this 2025 interview, LawDroid capabilities, Tennessee work and insurer savings are described as already available or experienced. Role transformation is expected to involve substantial short-term adjustment, followed by a richer experience, but there is no dated completion horizon. Proactive revenue growth depends on access to real-time organizational feedback and deep engagement with clients. Accessible guidance depends on reliable source material and adaptation to users' language and comprehension. Effective firm adoption requires a concrete value-producing problem, and professional reliance requires checking AI's work. Martin acknowledges early learning difficulties and imperfection rather than presenting the technology as universally reliable.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects span practicing lawyers, law firms, corporate clients, legal-aid users, courts and support staff.
pts.d: Lawyers receive task assistance but face changing skills and job definitions. Law firms face implementation and build-versus-buy decisions, possible reductions in reactive billed hours and opportunities for proactive client work. Corporate clients and their in-house legal functions are potential users of continuous legal analysis and implementation advice; Martin says lessons from access-to-justice work also apply to corporate legal and BigLaw settings. Legal-aid organizations and courts can extend conversational self-help and form assistance to more people, including those facing language or comprehension barriers or unaware of their legal issues. The insurer example concerns staff redeployment and support for a large lawyer network. Martin does not quantify effects by firm size or forecast specific staffing ratios or occupation-level job losses.
